CausalChain: DDR gene alterations -> Cytosolic DNA accumulation -> cGAS-STING pathway activation -> Interferon signaling -> PD-L1 upregulation -> T cell recruitment -> Tumor microenvironment conversion (cold to hot) -> Enhanced sensitivity to ICIs; PARP inhibition further intensifies DDR impairment -> Amplified immune activation
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancer, specific DDR deficiencies result in the accumulation of cytosolic DNA that activates the cGAS-STING pathway, driving strong interferon responses and subsequent PD-L1 upregulation which, in turn, enhances T cell infiltration. The application of cutting-edge genomic and transcriptomic profiling in real-time allows for the direct identification of BTC tumors exhibiting this DDR-immune activation signature. Importantly, treatment with PARP inhibitors is expected to further compromise DDR functionality, thereby intensifying the cGAS-STING-mediated immune cascade. When used in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors, this strategy is hypothesized to convert immunologically cold tumors into hot tumors, ultimately improving therapeutic outcomes in BTC. This revised hypothesis emphasizes continuous biomarker monitoring and an adaptive stratification strategy to fine-tune treatment regimens, ensuring clinical implementation is aligned with emerging technological capabilities.
Abstract: We propose that a subset of biliary tract cancers (BTCs) harbor specific deficiencies in DNA damage repair (DDR) genes that lead to the accumulation of cytosolic DNA. This genomic stress triggers the cGAS-STING pathway and induces a robust interferon response, which upregulates PD-L1 expression and facilitates T cell recruitment, thereby transforming the tumor microenvironment from immunologically cold to hot. Leveraging state-of-the-art genomic and transcriptomic profiling platforms, our approach enables the real-time identification of BTC cases exhibiting these molecular signatures. Furthermore, we hypothesize that the administration of PARP inhibitors will amplify DDR impairment, intensifying cGAS-STING-mediated immune activation. When combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), this regimen is expected to synergistically potentiate antitumor immunity. Our framework integrates precise molecular diagnostics with evolving therapeutic strategies, ensuring adaptive patient stratification and monitoring, and aims to provide a robust preclinical basis to advance this intervention in BTC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis linked DDR deficiencies to cGAS-STING activation and subsequent immune modulation, suggesting that PARP inhibitors would enhance this effect in BTC. The new hypothesis retains the original causal chain but refines it by explicitly incorporating advanced genomic and transcriptomic technologies for real-time tumor profiling and adaptive patient stratification. Additionally, while the original hypothesis assumed a direct conversion of cold to hot tumors via immune activation, the revised version emphasizes the necessity of iterative biomarker monitoring and preclinical validation, thereby addressing concerns of heterogeneity and mechanism specificity. The revised formulation remains novel, logically coherent, and practical, integrating each step of the original causal reasoning with contemporary technological applications to enhance clinical implementability.
